title: Scene SCENE-NW-01-01: Cabin of Boeing 747, landing at rain-swept Hamburg Airport, West Germany
statement: Upon touch-down in Hamburg, the cabin ceiling speakers broadcast an orchestral Muzak arrangement of The Beatles' 'Norwegian Wood'. Toru is seized by a sudden, violent psychosomatic shudder, clutching his head between his knees in his seat. When the flight attendant asks if he is sick, he replies that he is merely confused by memory.

source_claims.proposition: Establishes the entire novel as an act of memory retrieval and establishes that trauma is held somatically, waiting decades for a sensory trigger.
evidence: 'Are you all right, sir?' 'I'm fine, just feeling a little sick.'

relationships.details: Forces Toru to write the manuscript to honor his promise to Naoko.

materiality_reason: Narrative framing event; introduces central psychological trigger and lifelong promise.

title: Scene SCENE-NW-06-01: Kyoto train station to Ami Hostel, mountain bus route
statement: Toru receives a letter from Naoko inviting him to visit her at 'Ami Hostel' near Kyoto. Toru travels by train and a rickety mountain bus deep into the secluded cedar forests. He arrives at the communal sanctuary and meets Naoko's roommate, 38-year-old Reiko Ishida. Toru discovers the unique operational philosophy of Ami Hostel: it functions without locked gates, walls, or commercial medical billing. Residents and staff live together on equal terms, cultivating vegetable plots and workshops in a cashless barter economy where upkeep is paid through communal labor. Doctors and nurses wear ordinary clothes, eat identical communal meals, and openly acknowledge their own emotional vulnerabilities, rejecting the rigid hierarchical authority of conventional psychiatric institutions.

source_claims.proposition: Introduces Ami Hostel and Reiko Ishida, the essential third pillar of the novel.
evidence: Reiko's direct, humorous, chain-smoking warmth.

relationships.details: Toru gains access to Naoko's hidden world.

title: Scene SCENE-NW-06-03: Deep pine woods surrounding Ami Hostel
statement: Naoko and Toru walk alone in the forest. Naoko confesses her deepest sexual secret: that for all their years together, her body was completely incapable of sexual arousal with Kizuki (she remained dry and in pain). But with Toru on her 20th birthday, she became wet and open. This physical awakening filled her with unbearable guilt—as if she had betrayed Kizuki's memory and caused his death. Furthermore, Naoko confides a painful family history: when she was in the sixth grade (eleven years old), her beloved elder sister, who was seventeen, exceptionally brilliant, beautiful, and seemingly flawless, locked herself in her second-floor bedroom and hanged herself from the ceiling beam without warning or farewell note. Naoko was the one who unlocked the door and discovered her sister's dangling body. Naoko reflects that ever since that traumatic afternoon, she has felt an unexplained darkness lingering within her family lineage, fearing that she herself was destined to be drawn into that same silence. (Preserved as Naoko's personal narrative reflection, without imposing deterministic psychiatric labels).

title: Scene SCENE-NW-11-04: Futon in Toru's house in Kichijoji
statement: In the dark quiet following the music, Toru and Reiko hold each other and make love four times. It is not an act of romantic love, lust, or betrayal of Naoko; it is an ancient, somatic communion between two broken survivors clinging to warm, breathing human flesh to drive back the freezing chill of death.

source_claims.proposition: A crucial scene frequently misunderstood as simple infidelity; the text explicitly frames it as an exorcism of death through living touch.
evidence: Reiko: 'We are alive, Toru. We have to live.'

title: Scene SCENE-NW-11-06: Public glass telephone booth in a bustling Tokyo train station
statement: Toru enters a glass phone booth in a crowded Tokyo station and dials Midori's number. When she answers, he pours out his soul: he tells her he loves her, that he needs her, that he wants nothing else in the world except to live with her and start over. Midori goes silent for a long time, then asks quietly: 'Where are you now, Toru?' Toru looks out through the scratched glass at the rushing anonymous crowds and realizes with terror that he has no idea where he is. He calls her name repeatedly from the center of nowhere.

source_claims.proposition: The unforgettable, haunting climax of the novel that answers the beginning.
evidence: Midori: 'Where are you now, Toru?'
Toru: 'I called out to Midori again and again from the center of nowhere, calling into the void.'

relationships.target_source_unit_id: The ultimate callback to Naoko's meadow well: Toru has avoided falling, but is lost on the surface.

relationships.details: The novel ends on this indelible, ambiguous note of survival and dislocation.
